title: Ke Huy Quan Spent 20 Years Behind The Camera Before Hollywood Remembered He Was A Star
dek: From a 12-year-old who wasn't even supposed to audition, to stunt work on X-Men, to the Oscar stage — this is the wildest career arc in Hollywood, and every bit of it actually happened.

items.heading: He Wasn't Even Trying Out For Short Round — His Brother Was
items.text: Ke Huy Quan only showed up to the open casting call for Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom to support his older brother, who was the one actually auditioning. He spent the whole time coaching his brother from the sidelines, and casting directors got so intrigued by the kid giving directions that they pulled him in to read instead.

images.caption: The accidental audition that changed everything
Short Round, born out of an audition he never planned on taking

items.heading: Spielberg And Harrison Ford Basically Wrote The Card-Cheating Scene Around Him
items.text: Steven Spielberg loved Quan's natural energy so much that he and Harrison Ford improvised the now-classic scene where Short Round accuses Indy of cheating at cards. Quan beat out roughly 6,000 other kids for the role, and it launched him straight into The Goonies the following year as Data.

images.caption: The improvised card game that made Short Round a legend
Data, the gadget-obsessed Goonie, arrived just one year later

items.heading: Then The Roles Just... Stopped Coming
items.text: Despite starring in two of the decade's biggest movies before he was even a teenager, Quan found Hollywood had almost nothing left for him as an Asian actor once he grew up. By the late 1990s he'd stopped acting entirely and went back to school, earning a film degree from the USC School of Cinematic Arts.

images.caption: The child star who couldn't get a callback as an adult

items.heading: He Didn't Leave The Industry — He Just Went Behind The Camera
items.text: After graduating, Quan reinvented himself as a stunt coordinator and assistant director, working as an assistant action choreographer on the original X-Men under Corey Yuen. He later became an assistant director for legendary Hong Kong filmmaker Wong Kar-wai on 2046 — where he also met his future wife, Echo.

images.caption: One of the films where Quan worked stunts, not lines
The acclaimed director Quan assisted on 2046

items.heading: One Movie Made Him Want To Act Again
items.text: Watching Crazy Rich Asians in theaters in 2018 hit Quan hard — he's said he cried every time he saw it, partly out of joy and partly out of pure FOMO watching an all-Asian cast finally get their moment. That feeling pushed him to call up an agent for the first time in decades and ask to be represented again.

images.caption: The movie that convinced Quan to step back in front of the camera

items.heading: Two Weeks Later, The Daniels Called About Everything Everywhere All At Once
items.text: Almost immediately after re-signing with an agent, Quan was asked to audition for Waymond Wang in Everything Everywhere All at Once — a role written by directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert. Quan has said he loved the script instantly and felt like the multiversal husband role had been written specifically for him.

images.caption: The comeback role, decades in the making

items.heading: "Mom, I Just Won An Oscar" — And The Whole Room Lost It
items.text: At the 2023 Academy Awards, Quan won Best Supporting Actor and opened his speech by shouting out to his 84-year-old mother watching from home. He talked about starting his journey on a boat and spending a year in a refugee camp before ever imagining he'd stand on "Hollywood's biggest stage," calling it, simply, the American dream.

images.caption: The role that finally earned him the Oscar

items.heading: And He Hasn't Stopped Working Since
items.text: Quan followed his Oscar win by joining the MCU as the lovable engineer Ouroboros in Loki Season 2 — a role offered to him personally by Kevin Feige, whom Quan had actually met decades earlier as a fellow crew member on X-Men. He also reunited with Everything Everywhere co-stars Michelle Yeoh and Stephanie Hsu on Disney+'s American Born Chinese, playing a former child actor whose career arc mirrors his own.

images.caption: Ouroboros, the role Kevin Feige personally called him about
Playing a character with an eerily familiar career story
